name: Foot-in-the-Door
description: Securing agreement to a small initial request substantially increases compliance with a larger subsequent request, driven by a desire to act consistently with one's prior self-image.
design_relevance_note: The basis for progressive-commitment onboarding flows (small first action before a bigger ask) and micro-conversion funnel design.
myth_risk_note: Foot-in-the-door has foundational empirical support from Freedman & Fraser (1966) and a comprehensive mechanistic review by Burger (1999). However, the meta-analysis (Dillard et al. 1984) found the effect to be small, and more recent empirical work is limited. The technique is widely taught but actual effect sizes are modest and context-dependent.
prevalence_note: One of the most widely cited compliance techniques in both academic and popular persuasion-design writing.

findings.description: A review of the foot-in-the-door literature, including several meta-analyses, found the effect is real but not driven by one single mechanism — self-perception, consistency, commitment, conformity, reactance, and attribution processes all contribute. Their combined effects explain both why the technique succeeds under some conditions and fails, or even backfires, under others — the specific conditions most likely to produce a real effect are identified.
findings.source_title: The Foot-in-the-Door Compliance Procedure: A Multiple-Process Analysis and Review

findings.description: Once someone agreed to comply with a small initial request, they became significantly more likely to comply with a larger, related request later — even when a different person made the second request — the founding demonstration of the 'foot-in-the-door' compliance technique.
findings.source_title: Compliance Without Pressure: The Foot-in-the-Door Technique
findings.source_venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology

applications.title: 23andMe combining a preliminary survey with progress bars and social comparison
applications.description: 23andMe presents a short preliminary health survey, then encourages continued participation through progress bars and social comparison features showing how a user's answers compare to other participants -- layering the commitment/consistency principle with a competitive/social element to sustain engagement.
applications.ethical_note: Unlike the Fitbit entry in this same wave, this layers in social comparison on top of a genuine initial commitment, and the subject matter (personal health/genetic data) raises the stakes of sustained engagement pressure higher than a fitness app -- graded mixed rather than user_beneficial given that added social-pressure dimension, though nothing here indicates fabricated or deceptive framing.

applications.title: Fitbit displaying a user's stated fitness goal on their dashboard
applications.description: Fitbit asks new users to state a fitness goal on first launch, then keeps that goal visible on the dashboard going forward -- turning a small initial commitment (stating a goal) into an ongoing visual reminder intended to encourage consistent follow-through.
applications.ethical_note: The initial commitment (a fitness goal) is something the user genuinely chose and states voluntarily, and the ongoing reminder serves the user's own stated interest, not the company's -- a clean, low-risk application of the commitment/consistency principle.

applications.title: Freedman & Fraser's 1966 foot-in-the-door study: a small sign request more than quadrupling compliance with a large one
applications.description: Researchers asked residents to install a large, unattractive 'DRIVE CAREFULLY' sign on their front lawn -- only 17% agreed. But when a different group of residents had, two weeks earlier, first agreed to a small, easy request (a tiny 'BE A SAFE DRIVER' window sign), compliance with the later large-sign request jumped to 76%.
applications.ethical_note: The origin study for a technique now used deliberately in onboarding flows and progressive-commitment funnels (this graph's own Fitbit/23andMe examples) to convert small, low-friction agreements into larger ones the user might not otherwise have accepted -- worth naming as manipulative_risk since the mechanism relies specifically on the user not consciously recognizing that the earlier small request is functioning as a lever on the later, larger one.
